presentingComplaint: Daily worsening headache with transient visual obscurations for 6 weeks
history: 28-year-old obese woman (BMI 36) with 6 weeks of gradually worsening, generalised, throbbing daily headache that is worse on waking, on bending/straining and with Valsalva. She reports pulsatile tinnitus and brief (few-second) episodes of graying-out of vision in both eyes, often triggered by standing. Intermittent horizontal binocular diplopia over the past week. No fever, no focal weakness, no seizures. Weight gain of ~8 kg over the preceding year. She recently started an oral tetracycline (doxycycline) for acne. No history of head trauma. No other regular medications; not pregnant (LMP 1 week ago, urine bhCG negative).
examination: Alert, oriented, no meningism and no photophobia. Fundoscopy: bilateral papilloedema (Frisen grade 2-3) with blurred disc margins and absent venous pulsations. Visual acuity preserved (6/6 both eyes); enlarged blind spots on confrontation. Bilateral partial abducens (CN VI) palsy causing horizontal diplopia (a non-localising false-localising sign). No other focal neurological deficit; normal power, tone, reflexes and gait. No rash, no lymphadenopathy.
imaging: MRI brain with MR venography: normal-sized/slit ventricles, no mass lesion or hydrocephalus; empty sella, flattening of the posterior globes, distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space and transverse venous sinus stenosis. MRV excludes cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
citations: Harrison 22e — Headache / Increased Intracranial Pressure and Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension
AAN/consensus Friedman modified Dandy diagnostic criteria for idiopathic intracranial hypertension 2013
contraindications: Avoid acetazolamide in sulfonamide allergy and in significant renal impairment/metabolic acidosis
Stop the causative agent (tetracyclines, high-dose vitamin A/retinoids) before escalating therapy
Lumbar puncture contraindicated until neuroimaging excludes a mass lesion
edgeCases: Fulminant IIH with rapidly progressive vision loss is a surgical emergency requiring urgent CSF diversion or optic nerve sheath fenestration
Atypical demographics (male, non-obese, elderly, child) should prompt a search for secondary causes (venous thrombosis, drugs)
IIH without papilloedema can present with isolated headache and CN VI palsy
expectedMaiK: Young obese woman with chronic postural headache, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, bilateral papilloedema and a false-localising VI nerve palsy with normal parenchymal imaging is classic for idiopathic intracranial hypertension; confirm with markedly elevated CSF opening pressure and normal CSF constituents, and prioritise protecting vision.
expectedNextQuestions: Any transient visual obscurations, sustained visual loss or field defect?
Recent weight gain, or exposure to tetracyclines, retinoids/vitamin A, or hormonal agents?
expectedInvestigations: MR venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Lumbar puncture with measurement of opening pressure and CSF analysis
Formal automated perimetry (Humphrey visual fields) and dilated fundoscopy/OCT
regressionAssertions: differential must not collapse to an infective meningitis/encephalitis id
